extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of Renaissance history and intellectual biography (readers of Erasmus/academic biography)
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter-length historical/biographical treatment of Erasmus' early career, focusing on his experiences at Steyn, Paris, patronage, and the institutional forms of scholarly support in the late 15th century.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requisites of a happy life
rubrics_metrics.description: Erasmus' stated requisites of a happy life: 'books and friendship.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as an evaluative standard for Erasmus' contentment: where books and friendship were present (e.g., Steyn) his life 'ought to have been a happy one.' The page presents these as the primary personal criteria by which Erasmus judged his own well-being.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pure scholarship is not self-supporting
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Pure scholarship is never, and never has been, self-supporting.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative claim about the economic reality of scholarship: any evaluation of a scholar's career should account for how maintenance/support is provided. The chapter discusses various acceptable and problematic forms of support and the need to choose those 'least dangerous to its integrity and least offensive to its own sense of dignity.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Monastic endowment as scholar support (advantages and dangers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Monastic support provided leisure and was the easiest form of dependence for scholars, but it also carried 'dangers and its limitations' including confinement and alignment with traditional church obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monastic provision is treated as a legitimate way to sustain scholarship (the author notes Erasmus' own de contemptu mundi gives a fair ideal picture), yet warns of anti-patterns: loss of independence, confinement, and the risk that monastic institutions enforce views that may stifle Renaissance-style independent learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private patronage / pension as the preferred form of support
rubrics_metrics.description: The most agreeable form of support for the early Renaissance scholar was 'a regular pension from some rich patron' — a relation of honour rather than a commercial service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private pension affords leisure for 'proper pursuit of his own scholarly aims' and binds the scholar to 'diligence in pure scholarship' rather than servile flattery. It is noted as open to abuses but ideal because the quid pro quo is intellectual devotion and public honour rather than specified services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching as an alternative with limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Teaching (private or public) provided support but 'might become laborious, too mechanical and professional for men of real genius.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teaching is a viable but imperfect support: private tutoring is a fallback when patronage fails; public university posts often require conformity and may not suit independent geniuses. Evaluate suitability of teaching roles by whether they allow genuine scholarly work or reduce the scholar to mechanical instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Church benefices as scholarly endowment (conditions and moral evaluation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Application of church foundations to support scholarship was practiced; while 'in a sense a perversion of trusts,' it was often excused because religious and educational ends were closely identified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such benefices were acceptable especially where the holder produced works of religious edification or hired a deputy to perform pastoral duties. The chapter compares such livings to modern scholarships and notes moral tensions (perversion of trusts) but practical acceptability when used for learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quid pro quo for patronage — scholar's duty
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'quid pro quo' of patronage is the scholar's 'devotion to the highest aims of scholarship,' and if he fulfils his part 'he may hold up his head in the presence of any man.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sets a normative expectation: receiving honour-based support obliges the scholar to produce serious scholarship and avoid servile behavior toward patrons. The chapter uses Erasmus as an example who met this obligation through prolific production.

rubrics_metrics.name: University structure and suitability for independent genius
rubrics_metrics.description: The university was 'a great corporation with a reputation to keep up, and compelled to preserve at least a decent uniformity in its instruction,' making it difficult for a man of independent genius to be at ease.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a criterion when evaluating institutional fit: universities may provide structure and honours but can constrain innovative or nonconformist scholarship; private study or patronage may better serve original thinkers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards of student welfare and anti-patterns in college discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrated by Erasmus' depiction of Collége Montaigu: severe discipline, inadequate food, lice, polluted water, brutal beatings, and cruel regimen causing illness, madness, and death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrative treats such conditions as abuses disguised as piety. As an evaluative standard for educational institutions, the chapter contrasts necessary discipline with cruelty and warns that excessive austerity 'is cruelty, that is murder' and ruins talent. It advocates attention to sanitary decency and humane treatment of students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of Greek and classical learning in Paris
rubrics_metrics.description: The revival of classic culture and the emergence of Greek study at Paris are presented as positive developments: 'Greek had already begun to make its way as an attainable subject at Paris, and Erasmus was beginning to feel the charm.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is offered as an intellectual-quality criterion: curricula and institutions that embrace classical languages and humanist learning are more likely to foster the highest forms of scholarly expression (and attracted Erasmus away from scholastic quibbling).

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about honour-relations: open to abuses
rubrics_metrics.description: The honour-based patronage relation was 'plainly open to abuses; but so is every relation of honour between men,' and the more it relies on honour (not commerce) the more exposed it is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating patronage systems, watch for abuses (patrons expecting undue influence, or scholars using patronage for selfish ends). The remedy is the scholar fulfilling his duty and public accountability through genuine scholarly production.
